unit.title: 2D Shapes
unit.blurb: Properties of quadrilaterals, the parts of a circle, and rotational symmetry.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Identify, describe, classify and sketch quadrilaterals, including trapezia and kites, using their properties.

O2.t: Know the parts of a circle: centre, radius, diameter and circumference.

O3.t: Identify rotational symmetry in familiar shapes and find the order of rotational symmetry.

p: A **quadrilateral** is a 2D shape with **4 straight sides** and **4 angles**. The angles inside any quadrilateral add up to **360°**.
Quadrilaterals are named by their **properties**: equal sides, parallel sides, right angles and lines of symmetry.
**Parallel** lines never meet (marked with arrows). **Perpendicular** lines meet at a right angle.

p: A shape can belong to more than one family. A **square** is a special rectangle (4 right angles) **and** a special rhombus (4 equal sides).
Every rectangle, rhombus and square is a **parallelogram**, because each has two pairs of parallel sides.
A kite and a trapezium are **not** parallelograms.

lesson.t: How do I name a quadrilateral?
p: Step 1: Count the pairs of parallel sides: 2 pairs → parallelogram family; 1 pair → trapezium; 0 → look for a kite.
Step 2: Check the sides: all equal?
Step 3: Check the angles: all right angles?
Step 4: Give the most exact name (a shape with 4 equal sides and 4 right angles is a square).

lesson.q: A quadrilateral has 4 equal sides but no right angles. What is it?
steps: No right angles → not a square

lesson.q: 'A rectangle is a parallelogram.' True or false? Explain.
steps: A rectangle has 2 pairs of parallel sides
lesson.a: True – a rectangle has two pairs of parallel sides.

lesson.t: A trapezium has exactly one pair
p: A shape with two pairs of parallel sides is a parallelogram, not a trapezium. A trapezium has **exactly one** pair.

lesson.t: Use the properties in your answer
p: When asked to explain, name a property: 'It is a kite because it has two pairs of equal adjacent sides and no parallel sides.'

lesson.t: What are the parts of a circle?
p: The **centre** is the point in the middle; every point on the circle is the same distance from it.
The **radius** (r) is a straight line from the centre to the circle. The **diameter** (d) is a straight line across the circle **through the centre**.
The **circumference** is the distance all the way round the circle – its perimeter.

lesson.t: How are the radius and diameter linked?
p: A diameter is made of two radii, so **diameter = 2 × radius** and **radius = diameter ÷ 2**.

lesson.t: How do I draw a circle?
p: Use a **compass**. Open it to the length of the **radius** (not the diameter), put the point on the centre and turn the pencil all the way round.
To draw a circle with diameter 8 cm, open the compass to 4 cm.

lesson.t: How do I find a missing radius or diameter?
p: Step 1: Decide which length you are given.
Step 2: Radius given → double it for the diameter.
Step 3: Diameter given → halve it for the radius.
Step 4: Include the units.

Mark r or d on any circle diagram before you calculate – it stops you mixing them up.

p: A shape has **rotational symmetry** if it looks exactly the same in more than one position when it is turned about its centre.
The **order of rotational symmetry** is the number of times it looks the same in one full turn (360°).

lesson.t: What orders do common shapes have?
p: A shape that only fits once in a full turn has order **1** (this means **no** rotational symmetry).

lesson.t: Is rotational symmetry the same as line symmetry?
p: No. **Line symmetry** means one half is a mirror image of the other. Rotational symmetry is about **turning**.
A parallelogram has rotational symmetry of order 2 but **no** lines of symmetry. A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry **and** order n.

lesson.t: How do I find the order of rotational symmetry?
p: Step 1: Trace the shape (or imagine it) and mark one corner.
Step 2: Turn the tracing about the centre.
Step 3: Count how many times it fits exactly on the original before you get back to the start.
Step 4: That number is the order.

lesson.q: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a rectangle?
steps: Turn 90°: does not fit (long and short sides swap)

lesson.q: A pattern has order 4. One quarter is shaded. How many quarters are shaded altogether if the pattern is completed?
steps: Order 4: the design repeats 4 times in a full turn
Each turn of 90° copies the shaded quarter

p: Every shape fits at least once (at 360°), so the smallest order is **1**, never 0.
Count the turn back to the start only once: a square fits at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° – that is 4.
